dietEvidence.body: Herbivory is inferred from the dentition and jaw apparatus of pachycephalosaurs. No gut contents are known for Pachycephalosaurus, and the plants eaten are not preserved; the diet is a comparative inference.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A pachycephalosaur with a thick, domed skull roof and bony nodes around the dome. The dome is well preserved; its use in head-butting is debated.
summary: A pachycephalosaur with a thick, domed skull roof and bony nodes around the dome. The dome is well preserved; its use in head-butting is debated.

discovery.body: The species was first named Troodon wyomingensis by Gilmore, 1931; Brown & Schlaikjer, 1943 erected Pachycephalosaurus and combined it as P. wyomingensis. The holotype, USNM 12031, is a partial skull roof from the Lance Formation, Wyoming.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Several skull roofs and partial skeletons; the postcranium is less complete.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Hell Creek Formation, Montana and South Dakota records the species in the Late Cretaceous; the holotype, USNM 12031, comes from the Lance Formation of Wyoming. The numeric range used here is ≈68–66 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The frontal and parietal bones form a high dome, with a tuberculate squamosal shelf and a short, deep skull.

behaviour.body: The dome is preserved bone, but its use in head-butting is contested. Cranial pathologies have been read as combat trauma by some authors and as ontogenetic or display-related changes by others. Dracorex and Stygimoloch may be growth stages, but that synonymy is not universally accepted. No trackway or social group is known.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from several skull roofs and partial skeletons; the postcranium is less complete. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: Confidence is high for the dome and the 1931 species name, but lower for dome function, postcranial anatomy and the Dracorex/Stygimoloch synonymy. The name-bearing specimen, USNM 12031, is a partial skull roof, not a complete animal.
